opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's one of the more interesting open problems right now. Today, if you work with one agent, you can keep a pretty tight loop: you give it a task, it goes off and does some work, you check in, and you redirect it. That works fine when there's one, or maybe two or three. Once you have dozens of agents working on your behalf, you can't personally supervise each of them. So the questions become how you structure the work so that the pieces fit together, and how you avoid becoming the bottleneck yourself.

There are a few dimensions to it. The first is decomposition. You need to break a big goal into parts that are reasonably independent, with clear interfaces between them. That's not so different from how we organize large software engineering teams. When you're building a big system with hundreds of engineers, much of the art is in defining module boundaries so people can make progress without constantly stepping on each other. I think a lot of those lessons carry over to agents, and the agents may actually help with the decomposition itself.

The second is shared state and communication. If agent A changes an API that agent B depends on, how does B find out? You need some notion of a shared workspace, a record of decisions, and probably some agents whose job is coordination rather than doing the work. They review, integrate, run tests, and flag conflicts. That's a kind of management layer, and it's an interesting question how much of it can be automated well.

The third, and maybe the most important from the user's perspective, is the interface between the human and this whole collection of agents. You want to express intent at a fairly high level, and then be pulled in only when there's an ambiguity or a decision that really needs your judgment. Getting that calibration right is hard. If agents ask too often, you lose the benefit. If they ask too rarely, they go off and do a bunch of work in the wrong direction, which is wasted compute, or worse, they take actions you didn't want.

That ties into trust and permissions. When agents act on your behalf, sending emails, spending money, or modifying production systems, you need guardrails about what each one is allowed to do and some way to audit what happened afterward. Accountability matters more when the actions are distributed across many actors.

I'm fairly optimistic, though. The models are getting much better at long-horizon tasks, at knowing when they're uncertain, and at summarizing what they've done concisely. Those are exactly the capabilities you need for this kind of coordination to work. I can imagine a world fairly soon where one person effectively directs the equivalent of a small organization of agents, and that's a pretty profound shift in what an individual can get done.

r001.rationale: It describes the human being consulted when there is ambiguity or a decision needing judgment, and says calibrating how often agents ask is hard.

r002.rationale: It says improving model capabilities support coordination, but does not clearly suggest that human–agent interaction designs may change as those capabilities improve.

r003.rationale: It compares agent work to software teams defining module boundaries, but does not explain hierarchical coordination as arising from teams with limited interaction across them.

r004.rationale: It makes no comparison between five humans supervising 50 agents and five humans coordinating a 50-person software team.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think it's actually one of the most interesting problems right now, and in some ways it's a very old problem wearing new clothes. A lot of what we learned building large distributed systems at Google over the past couple of decades applies pretty directly. You have many independent workers, they have partial information, they can fail or produce bad output, and you need to compose their work into something coherent. The twist is that the workers are now non-deterministic and they communicate in natural language rather than in well-typed RPCs.

So I'd break the coordination challenges into a few pieces.

The first is decomposition. If you give one big task to a bunch of agents, someone has to decide how to split it up so that the pieces are mostly independent. In a MapReduce world you had a very clean abstraction for that. With agents, the dependencies between subtasks are often fuzzy. Two agents editing different parts of a codebase might both make a reasonable local decision that conflicts globally. So you want a decomposition where the interfaces between pieces are explicit and narrow, and ideally you want the system to recognize when a piece is too entangled to parallelize and just do it sequentially instead.

The second is shared state and communication. Right now a lot of multi-agent systems have agents talking to each other through long text transcripts, and that's really inefficient and lossy. I think we'll see much more structured intermediate representations, things like a shared plan, a set of constraints, a task graph with status, that agents read and write rather than re-deriving everything from a long context window. It's a bit like the difference between everyone shouting in a room versus having a shared whiteboard and a well-defined protocol.

The third is verification and trust. In a distributed system you assume components fail and you build in checksums, retries, and redundancy. With agents I think you want the same mindset. Don't trust a single agent's output. Have independent checks, whether that's tests, a separate reviewing agent, or just running things and seeing if they work. Redundant computation is cheap compared to the cost of a subtle error propagating through five downstream agents.

And then the fourth, which I think people underweight, is the human in the loop. If I have twenty agents working for me, I can't review twenty streams of activity. So the coordination layer also has to aggregate and summarize, surface the decisions that actually need my judgment, and quietly handle the rest. Figuring out that boundary, what rises to the level of asking the person versus what the system just resolves, is really a product and a research problem together.

The thing I find encouraging is that the models themselves are getting good enough to help with the coordination. You can have a model act as the orchestrator, notice when two subtasks are about to collide, and reorganize the work. Five years ago the hard part was getting any one agent to do anything useful. Now the hard part is more like a systems problem, and systems problems are something we have a lot of experience with.

r001.rationale: The response calls deciding what the system should resolve versus what should be raised to the person an open product and research problem.

r002.rationale: It says improving models can help coordinate agents, but does not suggest that human–agent interaction designs may change as model capabilities improve.

r003.rationale: It discusses decomposing tasks among agents, but does not explain hierarchy in conventional software organizations as teams working on separate system parts with limited interaction.

r004.rationale: It does not compare communication bandwidth for humans supervising virtual agents with humans coordinating software teams.

astra-6.text:
I think one of the interesting challenges is figuring out the right level of independence. You’d like to give a collection of agents a fairly high-level goal and have them divide up the work, but you also need them to recognize when their decisions affect each other. If two agents are changing different parts of a software system, those changes may look perfectly reasonable in isolation and still be incompatible.

So they need some way to share plans, communicate constraints, and check the combined result. You probably don’t want every agent talking to every other agent about every little decision—that would create a lot of overhead. You want communication to happen where there are dependencies.

And then there’s coordination with you. Which decisions should they make independently, and which should they bring back for clarification? Ideally, they handle a lot of the details, but surface the few questions where your preferences really matter. Getting that boundary right is going to be a big part of making these systems useful.

r001.rationale: The candidate asks which decisions agents should make independently and which they should bring to the human for clarification, identifying that boundary as a coordination question.

r002.rationale: It does not suggest that human–agent interaction designs may change as model capabilities improve.

r003.rationale: It discusses agents changing different parts of a system and needing to coordinate, but does not explain hierarchical coordination in conventional software organizations or limited interaction across teams.

r004.rationale: It makes no comparison involving five humans supervising 50 virtual agents and five humans coordinating a 50-person software team.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one of the interesting challenges is figuring out what can proceed independently and where you actually need coordination. If you have a number of agents working on a software project, for example, you’d like them to be able to explore different approaches or work on different components. But if they’re all modifying the same interface with different assumptions, you can end up doing a lot of work that doesn’t fit together.

So you need some combination of shared state, clear task boundaries, and ways to check the results. And you probably don’t want every agent communicating everything to every other agent. You want the relevant information to get to the right place, with relatively little overhead.

There’s also the question of when they should come back to you. Ideally, they resolve routine details themselves, but ask when there’s a meaningful ambiguity about what you want. Otherwise, having a hundred agents could turn into having a hundred things demanding your attention, which isn’t really the goal.

r001.rationale: It explicitly raises when agents should come back to the human, distinguishing routine details from meaningful ambiguities.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss how human–agent interaction designs might change as model capabilities improve.

r003.rationale: It discusses task boundaries and coordination, but not hierarchical coordination in conventional software organizations or limited interaction across teams.

r004.rationale: It does not compare communication bandwidth for humans supervising virtual agents versus coordinating a software team.
